name: Zero Point (Yumesamdong)
tagline: Where the civilian road ends, about 4,660 m above Lachung
meta_description: Zero Point (Yumesamdong), North Sikkim: snow at 4,660 m beyond Yumthang. Add-on cost from Lachung, permits, foreigner rules, altitude and safety advice.
summary: Zero Point, officially Yumesamdong, is the end of the civilian road about 23 km beyond Yumthang and roughly 45 km from Lachung, at about 4,660 m. It is a bare, snowy plateau visited as a paid add-on from Lachung, usually ₹3,000–4,000 per vehicle. Cold and altitude are serious here: stay short.
intro: Beyond Yumthang the road keeps climbing out of the rhododendron forest into open, stony country above the tree line. After about 23 km it reaches Yumesamdong, which every driver calls Zero Point: the place where civilian vehicles must stop. Beyond lies army territory and, further north, the Tibet border. There is nothing built here except a few seasonal stalls, and that is the point: snow on most days of the year, high peaks around you and thin, cold air.

For many Indian visitors Zero Point is the place to touch snow, even in May. The exact turning point moves with the season, depending on how far road crews and the army have cleared snow. In some weeks vehicles stop short; after heavy falls, the add-on is cancelled altogether. Your driver decides on the day based on conditions and orders, and arguing does not help.

At about 4,660 m, Zero Point is higher than anywhere most visitors have ever been. You arrive within a few hours of leaving Lachung at 2,700 m, which is a fast climb. Walk slowly, do not run or play hard in the snow, keep children warm and close, and stay no longer than 30 to 45 minutes. Anyone with a severe headache, breathlessness at rest or confusion should go down at once.

story.title: Why the road stops at Zero Point
story.text: North Sikkim's high valleys run up against the border with the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, and much of the land north of Yumthang is a military area. The name Zero Point simply marks the limit of civilian movement on the Lachung side, and the exact spot depends on season and orders. Wikipedia's article on Lachung notes that before China took control of Tibet in 1950, the village was a trading post between Sikkim and Tibet. Lachung and Lachen traders, and the herders of the high pastures, once moved goods and animals over these passes. After 1950, and especially after the 1962 India–China war, the border hardened and the trade routes closed. The Indian Army now keeps a forward presence in the valley, and the road to Yumesamdong exists largely because of that. Tourism came later, and remains tightly controlled through permits issued only to registered agents. When the army closes the road for an exercise or after snow, there is no appeal. Treat Zero Point as a privilege, not a promise.
story.source: Wikipedia, Lachung; Sikkim Tourism permit rules

little_known.fact: Zero Point is not a fixed spot: the place where civilian vehicles turn back moves with snow clearance and army orders, and in some weeks of winter the road is closed below it.
little_known.source: Local drivers and operators, as told locally

little_known.fact: At about 4,660 m, Zero Point is roughly 1,100 m higher than Yumthang and nearly 2,000 m higher than Lachung, a big climb in a single morning.
little_known.source: Wikipedia, Yumthang Valley of Flowers; altitude data

little_known.fact: The rivers draining Yumesamdong feed the Lachung Chu, which joins the Lachen Chu at Chungthang to form the Teesta, Sikkim's main river.

facts: ≈ 165 km · via a night in Lachung
Snow most of the year, road's end, high-altitude landscape
Protected area permit via a registered agent; foreigners ask us

highlights.title: Snow even in May
highlights.text: Zero Point usually has snow on the ground from autumn well into late spring, and often patches through summer. For many visitors it is the main reason to pay the add-on. Hire boots and coats in Lachung the evening before.

highlights.title: Above the tree line
highlights.text: The drive from Yumthang climbs from rhododendron forest into bare, stony country, a change of landscape that happens within half an hour. Watch the vegetation thin out as you climb towards 4,660 m.

highlights.title: The end of the road
highlights.text: This is as far as civilian vehicles may go on the Lachung side. Beyond lies army territory and the frontier. There is a strong sense of being at the edge of the map.

highlights.title: Clear autumn mornings
highlights.text: October and November mornings bring the clearest skies, with fresh snow on the peaks around Yumesamdong. They are also the coldest, often well below zero with wind.

highlights.title: Seasonal tea stalls
highlights.text: In the open season a few stalls sell tea, coffee, instant noodles and snacks. A hot cup at 4,660 m is part of the ritual; just remember that alcohol at this height is a bad idea.

how_to_reach.text: Book Zero Point as an extra with your Lachung driver, usually ₹3,000–4,000 per vehicle. You go on from Yumthang, about 23 km and 1 hour further, and return to Lachung by late morning.
In a private registered SUV the add-on is agreed with your agent in advance. The driver still needs the road to be open and the army to allow vehicles on the day.
Drive to Gangtok first (4.5–5 hours by NH10, or via Kalimpong when NH10 is closed), stay a night, go to Lachung the next day and to Zero Point the morning after.

costs: Boots and coat hire in Lachung
Tea or noodles at a stall
where_to_stay: Nobody sleeps at Zero Point: there is no accommodation and it would be dangerous at 4,660 m. Stay in Lachung, about 45 km below, and visit on an early morning drive. Families on a budget can choose a Lachungpa homestay; Snow Lion Mountain Resort and Fortuna Lachung are good value; Le Coxy Resort and Yarlam Resort suit travellers who want a warm room and a reliable packed breakfast before the 5 am departure.
tips: Decide on Zero Point at Yumthang: if anyone already has a headache there, skip it.
Stay 30–45 minutes, walk slowly and do not run or wrestle in the snow.
Wear sunglasses; snow glare at 4,660 m can burn eyes within an hour.
Agree the add-on price with your driver before leaving Lachung.
Carry your rubbish back; the plateau has no waste collection.

experiences.title: First snow at Zero Point
experiences.image_query: Zero Point North Sikkim snow tourists
experiences.summary: For many families, Zero Point is the first time they stand in deep snow. Done carefully, with warm clothes and a short stay, it is a joyful morning. Done carelessly, at 4,660 m, it is how people get altitude sickness.
body: The add-on begins at Yumthang, where your driver will ask whether you want to continue. The road climbs about 23 km above the forest into open, rocky country, and within an hour you are at the turning point, often with snow banks on both sides and white slopes rising around you. On clear mornings the light is dazzling.

Enjoy it gently. Walk, take photographs, build a small snowman with the children, but do not run, throw yourself into drifts or carry heavy loads. At 4,660 m each breath carries roughly 40 percent less oxygen than at sea level, and you climbed there in a few hours from 2,700 m. Most people feel short of breath; some feel headache or nausea. Those are signals to go down.

Wear hired boots and a long coat over your own warm layers, plus gloves, a cap and sunglasses. Keep children close and covered. Stay 30 to 45 minutes, then return to Yumthang and Lachung, where you will feel better within an hour of descending.

faqs.q: Is there always snow at Zero Point?
faqs.a: Snow is usual from about October to May and often lingers in patches into summer. In a dry autumn there may be less than expected, and after heavy falls the road may close. Snow cover is best in March to May. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Zero Point safe for children?
faqs.a: Children under five are not permitted in North Sikkim protected areas. Older children can go, but they are more likely than adults to hide symptoms, so ask them often how they feel. Keep them warm, do not let them run, and descend if they complain of headache or vomit.

faqs.q: How long should we stay at Zero Point?
faqs.a: About 30 to 45 minutes. That is enough for photos and a short walk. Longer stays at 4,660 m increase the risk of altitude sickness, especially for people who came up from the plains only a few days earlier. Your driver will also want to return before cloud and wind rise.

experiences.title: The drive above the tree line
experiences.cost: Included in the Zero Point add-on
experiences.image_query: road Yumthang to Zero Point Sikkim
experiences.summary: The hour from Yumthang to Zero Point is a lesson in altitude: rhododendron and fir forest give way to dwarf shrubs, then bare rock and snow. Ask your driver for two short stops to watch the landscape change.
body: Leaving Yumthang at about 3,564 m, the road climbs through the upper Shingba forest, where tree rhododendrons and firs thin out quickly. Above roughly 4,000 m the trees stop. Dwarf rhododendron and juniper hug the ground, and then even they give way to scree, boulders and, for much of the year, snow.

This is the only stretch of road in the Lachung valley where you see a full transition from forest to alpine desert in under an hour. Ask your driver to pull over safely at a wide point halfway up for photographs and a breath of air. Stay close to the vehicle; the road edges are loose and traffic, including army trucks, has right of way.
Coming down, the change runs in reverse, and many travellers notice their headache easing as the first trees reappear. That relief is the best reminder of how strongly altitude affects the body.

faqs.q: Is the road to Zero Point dangerous?
faqs.a: It is a narrow mountain road with steep drops, loose edges and, at times, snow and ice. Experienced local drivers handle it daily, and tourist vehicles travel in the safe morning hours. It is closed when conditions are bad. Wear seat belts and do not ask drivers to hurry.

faqs.q: Can we stop for photos on the way to Zero Point?
faqs.a: Short stops at safe, wide points are usually fine. Ask your driver, who knows where it is safe and where army rules forbid photography. Do not stop on bends, near military installations or in the path of convoys, and stay close to the vehicle.

faqs.q: Where does the tree line start on the Zero Point road?
faqs.a: Roughly around 4,000 m, a little above Yumthang. Trees thin through the upper rhododendron and fir forest and stop altogether, leaving low shrubs, grass and then bare rock. The exact line varies with slope and exposure.

experiences.title: Zero Point the altitude-smart way
experiences.summary: A simple plan to enjoy Zero Point without suffering: sleep low first, decide at Yumthang, climb with water and warmth, stay short and come down at the first serious warning sign. Our drivers follow this routine on every trip.
body: Altitude sickness does not care how fit you are. It depends mainly on how fast you climb. A typical North Sikkim trip goes from the plains to Gangtok (1,650 m), then Lachung (2,700 m), then Zero Point (4,660 m) within about three days. That is fast, so plan carefully: a night in Gangtok, a calm first evening in Lachung without alcohol, plenty of water and an early night.

Make the Zero Point decision at Yumthang. If anyone in the car already has a headache, nausea or unusual tiredness at 3,564 m, skip the add-on: they will feel worse higher up. At Zero Point, walk slowly, keep warm, eat something light and stay 30 to 45 minutes. Severe headache, breathlessness at rest, confusion or stumbling are emergencies: descend immediately.

Ask your doctor before the trip about acetazolamide and about any heart, lung or blood pressure conditions. Camphor, garlic and chocolates are popular remedies but do not prevent altitude sickness. The only reliable treatment is to go down.

faqs.q: Who should not go to Zero Point?
faqs.a: Children under five are not permitted. People with heart disease, severe lung conditions, uncontrolled blood pressure, pregnancy or recent surgery should consult a doctor first and may be advised not to go. Anyone already unwell at Yumthang should skip it.

faqs.q: Does camphor help with altitude sickness?
faqs.a: No. Sniffing camphor is a popular custom on Sikkim trips but there is no evidence it prevents or treats altitude sickness. What helps is a slower ascent, water, warmth, rest and, if symptoms become serious, going down. Ask your doctor about medicines before travelling.

faqs.q: What are the danger signs at Zero Point?
faqs.a: Severe or worsening headache, vomiting, breathlessness while resting, confusion, unsteady walking or unusual drowsiness. Any of these means descend at once with the vehicle and seek medical help in Lachung or Chungthang. Do not wait to see if it passes.

experiences.title: Tea at the last stall on the road
experiences.summary: In the open season a few stalls at Zero Point sell hot tea, coffee and instant noodles to visitors at the road's end. A warm drink here is a small ritual, and the stall keepers know the road better than anyone.
body: Seasonal stalls set up near the turning point when the road is open, selling tea, coffee, instant noodles, biscuits and snacks. Prices are higher than in Lachung, which is fair: everything comes up by road, and the people running them work long, cold days at 4,660 m.

A hot drink helps warm your hands and keeps you sipping fluid, which matters at altitude. Avoid alcohol, which some stalls sell: it dehydrates you and worsens altitude symptoms. Sit inside or in the lee of the stall out of the wind for ten minutes, then head back to the vehicle.

Stall keepers are a good source of road news: how far the snow has been cleared, whether the army has closed the area, how the weather looks. Pay in cash, keep your rubbish and carry it back to Lachung.

faqs.q: Is there food at Zero Point?
faqs.a: In the open season, a few seasonal stalls sell tea, coffee, instant noodles and snacks. They may be closed in deep winter or early spring. Carry snacks and water from Lachung in case nothing is open.

faqs.q: Should we drink alcohol at Zero Point?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol dehydrates you and makes altitude sickness more likely and worse, and Zero Point is about 4,660 m. Save any celebration for Gangtok. Stick to tea, coffee, soup and water at altitude.

faqs.q: Are there toilets at Zero Point?
faqs.a: Facilities are very basic or absent and change from season to season. Use the toilets in Lachung and at Yumthang before continuing, and carry tissue and a small bag for waste. Do not leave anything behind on the plateau.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Zero Point in Sikkim?
faqs.a: About 4,660 m (15,300 ft), according to most travel sources and consistent with elevation data for Yumesamdong. That is roughly 1,100 m above Yumthang and nearly 2,000 m above Lachung, climbed in a single morning, so altitude sickness is a real risk.

faqs.q: How much does Zero Point cost from Lachung?
faqs.a: It is a paid add-on to your Lachung package, around ₹3,000–4,000 per vehicle as an indicative 2026 figure, shared among everyone in the car. Agree the price with your driver or agent before leaving Lachung. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Zero Point open now?
faqs.a: The Lachung, Yumthang and Zero Point circuit reopened to tourists on 8 September 2025, as we understand it. Zero Point itself depends daily on snow clearance and army permission, and it is often shut in midwinter. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Zero Point?
faqs.a: Our facts memo lists Zero Point with Lachung and Yumthang as open to foreigners on a group protected area permit, but some operators report foreigners being stopped at Yumthang. Rules seem to vary in practice, so ask us before you plan. Gurudongmar is definitely closed to foreigners.

faqs.q: How far is Zero Point from Yumthang?
faqs.a: About 23 km, roughly 1 hour each way on a narrow mountain road. From Lachung the total is about 45 km. The full morning round trip from Lachung to Yumthang, Zero Point and back takes 5 to 6 hours.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Zero Point?
faqs.a: March to May for deep snow with milder days, and October to November for the clearest skies. December to February brings the most snow but frequent closures. In July and August the road is often affected by monsoon slides.

faqs.q: Why is it called Zero Point?
faqs.a: Zero Point is the common name for the place where civilian vehicles must stop on the road beyond Yumthang; its official name is Yumesamdong. Beyond lies a military area towards the Tibet border. The exact turning point shifts with season and army orders.

faqs.q: Can children go to Zero Point?
faqs.a: Children under five are not permitted in North Sikkim protected areas. Older children can go but should be watched closely, kept warm and not allowed to run in the snow. If a child has headache, vomiting or unusual sleepiness, return to Yumthang and Lachung straight away.

faqs.q: What should I wear to Zero Point?
faqs.a: Thermal innerwear, a warm fleece and a down jacket, plus a hired long coat and snow boots, gloves, a woollen cap and sunglasses. Sunscreen and lip balm are essential, as UV and glare are strong. Carry a refillable bottle of water.
